justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons were anchored primarily to the current market price or last observed level of approximately 39.9, reflecting a near-random-walk assumption for a financial asset or index over short time frames. At the one-day horizon, I expected minimal drift and set the point estimate essentially at the prevailing level, since any directional bias over a single trading session is difficult to justify without a strong catalyst. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate very slightly upward to 40.1, incorporating a modest positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run tendency of equity-like assets to trend upward, though this effect is negligible over such a short window. At the one-month horizon, the drift assumption contributes a bit more to the 40.5 estimate, but the dominant force is simply mean reversion toward the near-term level with a slight upward tilt.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using typical realized volatility for the asset class in question. At one day, historical daily volatility constrains the plausible range tightly, producing a roughly ±1.3-point interval at the 90% level. As the horizon extends to one week, volatility scales with the square root of time, widening the interval to roughly ±2.6 points. At one month, this scaling effect widens the interval considerably to roughly ±6.5 points, reflecting the compounding uncertainty over approximately 21 trading days. I also incorporated a small additional uncertainty premium to account for model uncertainty and the possibility of regime changes.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include macro surprises such as unexpected central bank policy shifts, geopolitical shocks, or sharp deteriorations in economic data releases. A sudden liquidity event or correlated forced selling across markets could drive prices well below the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where the interval is widest but tail risks can still be underestimated. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst — such as better-than-expected earnings, a policy easing surprise, or resolution of a geopolitical uncertainty — could push the price above the upper bound.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which underweight fat tails. Real financial markets exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning truly extreme moves — flash crashes, sudden sentiment reversals, or liquidity crises — occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. If any of these tail events materialize, the realized outcome could fall comfortably outside even the 90% confidence intervals I stated, especially at the one-week and one-month horizons where there is more time for compounding shocks to accumulate.
